title: Diseases of Blood Cell Production
subject: Hematopoietic System (HEME)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers disorders in which the marrow makes too few or too many blood cells: the microcytic anemias (iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia trait, sideroblastic anemia), the megaloblastic anemias of vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, aplastic anemia, the polycythemias, blood loss, neutropenia, and the leukemoid reaction. Board questions usually give iron studies, a smear, a cell count, or an erythropoietin level and ask for the cause or the next consequence. Each answer follows from one question: which raw material, signal, or stem cell has failed, and how does the marrow respond?
prerequisites: Hematopoiesis, the stem cell hierarchy, and growth factors such as erythropoietin and G-CSF (HE-1, HE-4)
Red cell indices: MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW, and the reticulocyte count (HE-2)
Folate and cobalamin coenzyme chemistry and thymidylate synthesis

connections.how: Hemolysis and blood loss both raise the reticulocyte count, while the production disorders here keep it inappropriately low.
Polycythemia vera, myelofibrosis, chronic myeloid leukemia, and myelodysplasia are clonal stem cell disorders that mimic or follow the conditions in this chapter.
Celiac disease, atrophic gastritis, ileal disease, and gastrectomy cause iron, B12, and folate deficiency by removing the absorptive sites.

connections.to: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control (UR-7)
connections.how: Renal peritubular cells sense oxygen delivery and release erythropoietin, so kidney disease and kidney tumors change red cell production.
Autoimmunity causes pernicious anemia, most aplastic anemia, and immune neutropenia, and inflammatory cytokines drive anemia of chronic disease.

sections.title: Iron deficiency anemia: causes and laboratory profile

blocks.text: The body has no regulated way to excrete iron, so iron balance is controlled at absorption. An adult absorbs about 1 to 2 mg per day in the duodenum and upper jejunum, which matches obligatory losses from shed skin and gut cells; menstruation adds an average of about 0.5 to 1 mg per day. Nonheme ferric iron (Fe3+) is reduced at the brush border by duodenal cytochrome b, enters through divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1), and leaves the enterocyte through ferroportin, after which hephaestin reoxidizes it for binding to transferrin. Gastric acid keeps iron soluble and favors reduction, so achlorhydria and gastrectomy impair uptake, and celiac disease destroys the duodenal surface that absorbs it.

Iron deficiency anemia, the most common anemia worldwide, appears when losses or needs exceed this small intake. In adults the usual cause is chronic blood loss, and in a man or a postmenopausal woman a gastrointestinal source such as colorectal cancer must be considered. Pregnancy needs about 1 g of extra iron in total for the expanded red cell mass, placenta, and fetus.

blocks.title: Causes of iron deficiency
rows: Menorrhagia; peptic ulcer, colorectal cancer, angiodysplasia; hookworm infection worldwide
Infants fed mostly cow's milk, restrictive diets, poor diet in older adults
Celiac disease, gastrectomy or bypass of the duodenum, achlorhydria from atrophic gastritis
Pregnancy and lactation, infancy and adolescent growth
blocks.caption: Blood loss is the leading cause in adults; poor intake matters most when needs are high.

blocks.text: Deficiency develops in stages. Stores are used first, so ferritin falls while hemoglobin is still normal; ferritin is the earliest and most specific single test. Next, transport iron falls. Hepatocytes respond to low iron by making more transferrin, so TIBC rises while serum iron falls and transferrin saturation (serum iron divided by TIBC) drops. Ferrochelatase then inserts zinc in place of the missing iron, so zinc protoporphyrin rises, and erythroblasts display more transferrin receptors, raising soluble transferrin receptor. Hepcidin is suppressed, which maximizes absorption.

Only then does anemia appear. Erythroid precursors are thought to keep dividing until they reach a set hemoglobin concentration, so when hemoglobin synthesis lags they divide an extra time and the cells come out small (microcytic, MCV below about 80 fL) and pale (hypochromic, central pallor wider than one third of the cell). Because these small cells mix with older normal cells, the RDW rises early, which helps separate iron deficiency from thalassemia trait. The smear may show elongated pencil cells, and a reactive thrombocytosis is common. Iron-dependent enzymes in rapidly renewing epithelia also fail, producing glossitis, angular cheilitis, and spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia); pica, especially for ice, is a classic but poorly explained feature.

blocks.title: Iron studies: what each test measures
rows: Low; below about 15 ng/mL is diagnostic
blocks.caption: Ferritin reflects stores, TIBC reflects transferrin, and saturation reflects how much transport iron is available to the marrow. Ranges vary by laboratory.

sections.title: Separating the microcytic anemias with iron studies and the smear

blocks.text: Hemoglobin needs iron, protoporphyrin, and globin, so a microcytic anemia means one of four steps has failed: iron supply (iron deficiency), iron release from stores (anemia of chronic disease), globin synthesis (thalassemia), or heme synthesis (sideroblastic anemia). Iron studies and the smear identify the step.

blocks.title: How inflammation restricts iron
steps: Infection, autoimmunity, or cancer raises IL-6
IL-6 induces hepcidin synthesis in hepatocytes
Hepcidin binds ferroportin, which is internalized and degraded
Macrophages and enterocytes cannot export iron
Serum iron falls; stored iron and ferritin stay normal or high
Iron-restricted erythropoiesis produces anemia
blocks.caption: Hepcidin withholds iron from the marrow, which likely evolved to deprive microbes of iron.

blocks.text: In anemia of chronic disease, iron is present but locked away. Serum iron falls within hours of inflammation. Ferritin is normal or high because iron accumulates in macrophages and because ferritin is itself an acute phase reactant, while transferrin is a negative acute phase reactant, so TIBC is low. Inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1, tumor necrosis factor, and interferon-gamma also blunt erythropoietin release and the marrow response to it, and red cell survival is mildly shortened. The anemia is usually mild and normocytic, becoming mildly microcytic when it lasts.

Thalassemia trait leaves iron handling normal. Reduced globin synthesis makes many small cells, so the red cell count is normal or high and the microcytosis is out of proportion to a mild anemia; a Mentzer index (MCV divided by red cell count in millions per µL) below about 13 favors thalassemia. Cells are uniformly small, so the RDW is usually normal, and target cells form because the membrane is large relative to the hemoglobin it holds. Beta thalassemia trait raises hemoglobin A2 above about 3.5%, while alpha trait gives a normal adult electrophoresis.

In sideroblastic anemia, iron reaches the erythroblast but cannot enter protoporphyrin, so it collects in mitochondria. Serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation are high, TIBC is low or normal, and Prussian blue staining of marrow shows ringed sideroblasts. The smear is often dimorphic, with a mixed population of hypochromic and normal cells, and may show Pappenheimer bodies (iron granules).

blocks.title: Iron studies in microcytic anemia
rows: High RDW, pencil cells, high platelets
Target cells, high red cell count, normal RDW
Dimorphic cells, ringed sideroblasts in marrow
blocks.caption: TIBC moves opposite to ferritin in iron deficiency and in the same direction in anemia of chronic disease.

blocks.title: Worked example: inflammation plus blood loss
blocks.text: A woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 76 fL, serum iron 30 µg/dL, TIBC 260 µg/dL, and ferritin 70 ng/mL. Ferritin of 70 would exclude iron deficiency in a healthy person, but inflammation raises ferritin independent of stores, so a normal value no longer proves adequate iron. Clues to added iron deficiency are a TIBC that is not low, a high RDW, and microcytosis more marked than inflammation alone usually causes. A high soluble transferrin receptor would confirm it, because erythroblasts starved of iron increase their receptors, whereas hepcidin-restricted marrow in pure anemia of chronic disease does not. Many references accept ferritin up to about 100 ng/mL as compatible with iron deficiency when inflammation is present.

blocks.predict: Predict the hepcidin level and the rate of duodenal iron absorption in iron deficiency compared with anemia of chronic disease.
blocks.explain: Iron deficiency suppresses hepcidin, so ferroportin stays on enterocytes and absorption rises; inflammation raises hepcidin, so ferroportin is degraded and absorption falls even though the patient is anemic.

sections.title: Causes of sideroblastic anemia and the heme effects of lead

blocks.text: Heme synthesis begins and ends in the mitochondrion. Aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS) condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA into aminolevulinic acid (ALA), using pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6) as cofactor; this is the rate-limiting step. The middle steps occur in the cytosol, and the last enzyme, ferrochelatase, inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX back in the mitochondrion. Erythroblasts use their own isoform, ALAS2, whose translation increases when iron is plentiful. When heme synthesis fails, iron keeps arriving in mitochondria that cannot use it, and these iron-loaded mitochondria, clustered around the nucleus, form the ringed sideroblast.

blocks.title: Heme synthesis and the sites of lead inhibition
steps: Glycine plus succinyl-CoA (mitochondrion)
ALA synthase, needs vitamin B6, forms ALA
ALA dehydratase forms porphobilinogen (cytosol); lead inhibits
Porphobilinogen converted through porphyrinogens
Protoporphyrin IX formed (mitochondrion)
Ferrochelatase inserts Fe2+ to make heme; lead inhibits
blocks.caption: Blocks after iron delivery trap iron in mitochondria; lead also leaves ALA and protoporphyrin to accumulate.

blocks.title: Causes of sideroblastic anemia
rows: Reduced erythroid ALA synthase; many mutations lower affinity for pyridoxal phosphate
Hereditary, mostly males, microcytic; some respond to high-dose pyridoxine, reflecting the cofactor defect
Mitochondrial toxin; impairs pyridoxal phosphate formation and heme enzymes
Common acquired cause; reverses with abstinence
Too little cofactor for ALA synthase
Often drug-induced, classically by isoniazid, which binds and depletes B6
Basophilic stippling, high zinc protoporphyrin and urinary ALA
Copper deficiency (including zinc excess); clonal defect in myelodysplastic syndrome
Myelodysplasia gives a macrocytic or dimorphic picture in older adults
blocks.caption: The main hereditary form affects the first step; most acquired forms are toxic or nutritional.

blocks.text: Lead binds sulfhydryl groups and displaces zinc from ALA dehydratase, so ALA accumulates in blood and urine. It also inhibits ferrochelatase, so protoporphyrin accumulates and zinc is inserted in place of iron, giving a high zinc protoporphyrin (free erythrocyte protoporphyrin). Zinc protoporphyrin also rises in iron deficiency, because ferrochelatase lacking iron uses zinc, so a high value supports lead exposure only with a normal ferritin or a raised blood lead level, which is the diagnostic test.

Lead also inhibits pyrimidine 5' nucleotidase, the enzyme that clears pyrimidine nucleotides from degraded ribosomal RNA as reticulocytes mature. Undegraded ribosomes aggregate into coarse blue dots on Wright stain, called basophilic stippling. The anemia of lead poisoning is mild, hypochromic, and microcytic or normocytic, with a hemolytic component from damaged membranes and enzymes; ringed sideroblasts are present in some patients but not all. Lead's neurologic and renal effects are taught with those systems.

sections.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency, megaloblastic anemia, and subacute combined degeneration

blocks.text: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) comes only from animal foods. Acid and pepsin release it from food protein, and it binds haptocorrin (R-binder) from saliva. In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin and B12 binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells. The complex is taken up by the cubilin receptor in the terminal ileum, and transcobalamin carries B12 in plasma. Body stores of about 2 to 5 mg, mostly in the liver, far exceed a daily need of a few micrograms, so deficiency takes years to appear.

blocks.title: Causes of B12 deficiency by the step that fails
rows: Strict vegan diet without fortified foods
Achlorhydria, atrophic gastritis, long-term acid suppression
Pernicious anemia; total or proximal gastrectomy
Ileal resection, Crohn disease of the terminal ileum
Fish tapeworm Dibothriocephalus (formerly Diphyllobothrium) latus; small bowel bacterial overgrowth
blocks.caption: Every step of the absorption pathway is a possible point of failure.

blocks.text: Pernicious anemia is autoimmune atrophic gastritis of the body and fundus. CD4 T cells and antibodies against the parietal cell proton pump (H+/K+ ATPase) destroy parietal cells, and antibodies against intrinsic factor block B12 binding; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are less sensitive but highly specific. Loss of acid causes antral G cell hyperplasia with high gastrin and raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumors, and the disease clusters with other autoimmune disorders such as Hashimoto thyroiditis. The fish tapeworm, acquired from raw or undercooked freshwater fish, absorbs B12 in the small intestine before the host can.

blocks.title: From B12 deficiency to megaloblastic anemia
steps: Methionine synthase lacks methylcobalamin
Folate is trapped as methyl-THF
Less methylene-THF for thymidylate synthase
dTMP falls; DNA synthesis slows
Nucleus matures late while cytoplasm grows
Megaloblasts die in marrow; macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils
blocks.caption: The methyl-folate trap explains why B12 deficiency produces the same blood picture as folate deficiency.

blocks.text: B12 serves two enzymes. Methionine synthase transfers a methyl group from methyl-tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, forming methionine and regenerating tetrahydrofolate (THF); without it, folate is trapped and thymidine synthesis fails, so DNA replication lags behind RNA and protein synthesis in every dividing cell. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase converts methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA; without it, methylmalonic acid rises. Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid are therefore both high. Many megaloblasts die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis), raising LDH and indirect bilirubin and lowering haptoglobin, while the reticulocyte count stays low. The blood shows oval macrocytes (MCV above 100 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils (commonly defined as at least 5% with five lobes or any with six), and often pancytopenia; the marrow is hypercellular. Glossitis reflects the same failure in the oral epithelium.

Subacute combined degeneration is symmetric demyelination of the dorsal columns (loss of vibration and position sense, positive Romberg sign) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses), often with peripheral neuropathy and cognitive change. Low S-adenosylmethionine impairs methylation of myelin proteins and lipids, and accumulated methylmalonyl-CoA may produce abnormal fatty acids in myelin. Neurologic damage can appear before or without anemia and may be permanent.

blocks.predict: A patient with unrecognized B12 deficiency takes high-dose folic acid. What happens to the anemia and to the spinal cord lesions?
blocks.explain: Folic acid is reduced to THF through dihydrofolate reductase, bypassing the methyl-folate trap, so thymidine synthesis and the anemia improve. Methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase still lack B12, so demyelination continues while the blood count hides it.
blocks.check: Compare with the two B12-dependent reactions and the flow above.

blocks.text: Folate is found in leafy vegetables, legumes, and liver, is destroyed by prolonged cooking, and is absorbed in the jejunum after brush border enzymes cleave its polyglutamate tail. Body stores last only about 3 to 4 months, so deficiency develops far faster than B12 deficiency. Its blood and marrow findings are the same megaloblastic picture, because both deficiencies cut the supply of methylene-THF to thymidylate synthase.

blocks.title: Causes of folate deficiency
rows: Alcohol use disorder, poor diet in older or low-income adults
Pregnancy, chronic hemolytic anemia (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis), exfoliative skin disease
Celiac disease, tropical sprue, extensive jejunal disease
Methotrexate (and weaker human effects of trimethoprim and pyrimethamine) inhibit dihydrofolate reductase
blocks.caption: Alcohol lowers folate by several routes at once: intake, absorption, hepatic storage, and enterohepatic cycling.

blocks.text: Methotrexate shows the mechanism clearly. Thymidylate synthase oxidizes methylene-THF to dihydrofolate (DHF) as it makes dTMP, and dihydrofolate reductase must reduce DHF back to THF. Blocking that enzyme depletes active folate in any rapidly dividing cell, producing megaloblastic marrow and mucositis.

blocks.title: B12 versus folate deficiency
rows: Time for stores to run out
blocks.caption: Methylmalonic acid is the biochemical test that separates the two deficiencies.

blocks.text: Not every macrocytosis is megaloblastic. In nonmegaloblastic macrocytosis DNA synthesis is normal, the cells are round rather than oval, neutrophils are not hypersegmented, and the marrow is not megaloblastic. Liver disease raises cholesterol and phospholipid in the red cell membrane, enlarging the cell and producing target cells. Alcohol is directly toxic to erythroid precursors and raises the MCV even with normal folate and a normal liver, although all three problems often coexist. Reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells, so a brisk reticulocytosis after hemorrhage or in hemolysis raises the MCV; the smear shows polychromasia and the reticulocyte count is high. Hypothyroidism is another common cause.

blocks.title: Megaloblastic versus nonmegaloblastic macrocytosis
rows: Round macrocytes; target cells in liver disease
Normal or low; high in reticulocytosis
blocks.caption: Look at the smear and the reticulocyte count before attributing a high MCV to a vitamin deficiency.

sections.title: Aplastic anemia: failure of the stem cell

blocks.text: Aplastic anemia is failure of the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell, giving pancytopenia with a hypocellular marrow in which fat replaces hematopoietic tissue. Because the defect lies above every lineage, red cells, granulocytes, and platelets fall together, and the reticulocyte count is low. That combination separates it from peripheral destruction or sequestration, where the marrow is full and working.

Most acquired cases are immune. Activated cytotoxic T cells recognize stem and progenitor cells, and interferon-gamma and tumor necrosis factor drive them into apoptosis; the disease often responds to immunosuppression, which supports this mechanism. Other causes injure stem cells directly. Some agents act in a dose-dependent, predictable way (ionizing radiation, alkylating agents and other cytotoxic chemotherapy, benzene), while others cause rare idiosyncratic aplasia (chloramphenicol, carbamazepine, some sulfonamides). Hepatitis-associated aplasia appears weeks to months after an acute hepatitis, usually one not caused by hepatitis A, B, or C. A minority of patients carry inherited telomere maintenance defects.

Fanconi anemia is an inherited, mainly autosomal recessive defect in repair of DNA interstrand crosslinks (FANC gene pathway). Stem cells accumulate DNA damage and die, so marrow failure usually appears in childhood. Associated findings include short stature, absent or abnormal thumbs and radii, cafe au lait spots, and renal anomalies, and chromosome breakage increases when cells are exposed to crosslinking agents such as diepoxybutane or mitomycin C, which is the diagnostic test. Survivors have a high risk of acute myeloid leukemia and squamous cell carcinomas.

Manifestations follow the missing cells: anemia causes fatigue and pallor, thrombocytopenia causes petechiae and mucosal bleeding, and neutropenia causes bacterial and fungal infection. The MCV is normal or mildly high. The spleen, liver, and lymph nodes are not enlarged, because the marrow is empty rather than infiltrated and there is no extramedullary hematopoiesis; splenomegaly points to another diagnosis. Aplastic anemia may later evolve into paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria or myelodysplasia, reflecting clonal escape from immune attack. Parvovirus B19 infects only erythroid progenitors, so it causes pure red cell aplasia rather than pancytopenia.

blocks.title: Telling aplastic anemia from other causes of pancytopenia
rows: Infiltrated or fibrotic, often a dry tap
Cells pooled in the spleen, marrow production normal
blocks.caption: A marrow biopsy is required: the peripheral count alone cannot show whether production is absent or cells are being lost.

sections.title: Polycythemia vera versus secondary and relative polycythemia

blocks.text: Polycythemia means a high hemoglobin or hematocrit, above about 16.5 g/dL or 49% in men and 16 g/dL or 48% in women. The first question is whether the red cell mass is truly increased or only concentrated by lost plasma. The second is what erythropoietin is doing, because erythropoietin is the normal controller of red cell mass.

blocks.title: Oxygen sensing and erythropoietin feedback
steps: Oxygen delivery to the kidney falls
HIF-2 alpha escapes degradation in peritubular interstitial cells
Erythropoietin is released into blood
Erythroid progenitors survive and divide
Red cell mass and oxygen delivery rise
HIF is degraded and erythropoietin falls
blocks.caption: The loop senses oxygen delivery, not hemoglobin; the liver adds a smaller share of erythropoietin in adults.

blocks.text: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm in which the loop is bypassed at the progenitor. About 95% of patients carry JAK2 V617F, which disables the autoinhibitory pseudokinase domain of JAK2, the kinase bound to the erythropoietin receptor; most of the rest have JAK2 exon 12 mutations. Signaling through STAT5 continues without hormone, so the clone expands independently and normal feedback drives erythropoietin low or low normal. JAK2 also serves the thrombopoietin and G-CSF receptors, so platelets and neutrophils often rise too, and the marrow shows proliferation of all three lineages. Clinical clues are facial plethora, splenomegaly from extramedullary hematopoiesis, a high LAP score, and aquagenic pruritus, itching after a warm bath from histamine released by the expanded basophil and mast cell population.

In secondary polycythemia the clone is normal and erythropoietin is high. It is appropriate when tissue oxygen delivery is truly low: chronic lung disease, sleep apnea, high altitude, right-to-left shunts, and high oxygen affinity hemoglobins. Smoking belongs here because carbon monoxide occupies hemoglobin and shifts the dissociation curve left; standard pulse oximetry misreads carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin and may look normal, while co-oximetry shows the true saturation. Erythropoietin is inappropriate when it is secreted without hypoxia, as by renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, or uterine leiomyoma, or by renal cysts and hydronephrosis that compress local tissue; oxygen saturation is normal. Exogenous erythropoietin and androgens also raise red cell mass.

Relative polycythemia has a normal red cell mass and a reduced plasma volume, from dehydration, vomiting and diarrhea, diuretics, or burns. Erythropoietin is normal and the hematocrit corrects when plasma volume is restored.

blocks.title: Types of polycythemia
rows: JAK2 V617F neoplasm; high white cells and platelets, splenomegaly
Low (carbon monoxide: low by co-oximetry, pulse oximetry may read normal)
Lung disease, sleep apnea, altitude, cyanotic heart disease, smoking
Renal cell or hepatocellular carcinoma, hemangioblastoma, leiomyoma, renal cysts
blocks.caption: Erythropoietin is the branch point: low in PV, high in secondary forms, normal in relative polycythemia.

blocks.predict: A man with a hematocrit of 58% has normal arterial oxygen saturation by co-oximetry and a high erythropoietin. What should be searched for, and why is PV unlikely?
blocks.explain: High erythropoietin without hypoxia means a source is secreting it autonomously, most often a renal cell or hepatocellular carcinoma. In PV the clone grows without erythropoietin and feedback suppresses it.
blocks.check: Compare with the feedback cycle and the types of polycythemia table.

blocks.text: Blood viscosity rises steeply, not linearly, as hematocrit increases. By Poiseuille's law, flow varies inversely with viscosity, so above a certain hematocrit the extra oxygen carried per milliliter is outweighed by slower flow, and delivery to the brain, heart, and digits falls. Hyperviscosity explains headache, dizziness, tinnitus, blurred vision, and angina. Thrombosis is the leading cause of illness and death in PV, and it reflects more than viscosity: clonal platelets and neutrophils are activated and adhere to endothelium, and high platelet counts add to the risk.

Thrombosis affects arteries (stroke, transient ischemic attack, myocardial infarction) and veins (deep venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism). PV and other JAK2 neoplasms are a leading identified cause of thrombosis in unusual abdominal sites: hepatic vein thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome, with painful hepatomegaly and ascites) and portal or mesenteric vein thrombosis. Such a clot may be the first sign of PV, and blood counts can look only mildly abnormal because the expanded plasma volume and sequestration in a large spleen dilute them.

Erythromelalgia is burning pain, warmth, and redness of the hands and feet, made worse by heat, caused by platelet-rich microthrombi and inflammation in small arterioles; it can progress to digital ischemia. High cell turnover increases purine breakdown, so uric acid rises, causing gout and urate stones. Histamine from basophils and mast cells contributes to pruritus and peptic ulcer. Paradoxically, bleeding can occur when platelet counts are extremely high, because platelets adsorb and clear large von Willebrand factor multimers (acquired von Willebrand syndrome).

PV is a clonal stem cell disease and evolves over years. In post-PV myelofibrosis, the spent phase, clonal megakaryocytes release fibrogenic cytokines such as transforming growth factor beta and platelet-derived growth factor, and fibroblasts lay down collagen. The marrow fails, the hematocrit falls, and hematopoiesis moves to the spleen and liver, producing massive splenomegaly, teardrop cells, and a leukoerythroblastic smear (nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes). A smaller fraction of patients transform to acute myeloid leukemia, with a poor outlook.

blocks.title: Complications of polycythemia vera by mechanism
rows: Stroke, transient ischemic attack, myocardial infarction
Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal or mesenteric vein thrombosis, DVT
Burning, red, warm hands and feet worsened by heat
Purine catabolism from expanded cell mass
Falling counts, massive spleen, teardrop cells, blasts
blocks.caption: Thrombosis is the main early danger; fibrosis and leukemia are late.

blocks.text: Hemoglobin and hematocrit are concentrations. In acute hemorrhage, red cells and plasma are lost together, so the concentration right after bleeding is normal or near normal even when the loss is large; the early clues are tachycardia, hypotension, and low urine output, not the blood count. The count falls only as plasma volume is restored. Lower capillary hydrostatic pressure draws interstitial fluid into the vessels (transcapillary refill), and the kidney retains sodium and water through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and antidiuretic hormone. This takes about 1 to 3 days.

blocks.title: Time course after acute hemorrhage
steps: Whole blood lost; hemoglobin concentration unchanged
Hours: neutrophilia and thrombocytosis from stress and demargination
Hours to 3 days: fluid refill dilutes red cells; hemoglobin falls
Erythropoietin rises within hours of reduced oxygen delivery
About 3 to 5 days: reticulocytosis appears
About 7 to 10 days: reticulocyte count peaks
About 3 to 6 weeks: red cell mass restored if iron is adequate
blocks.caption: The marrow response lags because progenitors need several days to mature into reticulocytes.

blocks.text: The anemia is normocytic and normochromic, and iron studies are normal unless stores were already low. Once the marrow responds, polychromasia and a high reticulocyte count appear, and because reticulocytes are large the MCV may rise slightly. A brisk reticulocyte response shows that the marrow, iron supply, and erythropoietin axis are intact, which separates blood loss and hemolysis from the production disorders in this chapter.

blocks.title: Worked example: why the first hematocrit underestimates the loss
blocks.text: A man with a blood volume of 5.0 L and a hematocrit of 45% has 2.25 L of red cells. He rapidly loses 1.0 L of blood, which takes 0.45 L of red cells and 0.55 L of plasma. The remaining 4.0 L has 1.8 L of red cells, and 1.8 divided by 4.0 is still 45%. Over the next 1 to 3 days, refill and renal retention return his blood volume to about 5.0 L without adding red cells. His hematocrit becomes 1.8 divided by 5.0, or 36%. The 20% loss of red cell mass was present from the first minute but became visible only after plasma volume was restored.

Chronic blood loss behaves differently. Each milliliter of blood at a normal hemoglobin carries about 0.5 mg of iron, so losing even a few milliliters a day from the gut or through heavy menstruation exceeds the 1 to 2 mg absorbed. The hemoglobin stays normal while stores drain, then an iron deficiency anemia develops with the profile in C01, and the reticulocyte count is inappropriately low because iron limits the response. Blood that escapes into tissues or body cavities, as in a large hematoma, is broken down by macrophages and its iron is reused, so internal bleeding does not cause iron deficiency.

Neutrophils are made in the marrow over about two weeks, circulate for only hours, and are split between a circulating pool and a marginated pool adherent to vessel walls. The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) equals the white cell count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands. Neutropenia is an ANC below about 1500/µL in adults, graded as mild (1000 to 1500), moderate (500 to 1000), or severe (below 500/µL). Agranulocytosis is a severe, usually abrupt, loss of neutrophils, often defined as an ANC below 500/µL.

Infection risk climbs as the ANC falls and becomes high below 500/µL, especially when neutropenia is prolonged. Infections come mainly from the patient's own flora: gram-negative enteric bacilli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, coagulase-negative staphylococci, and streptococci, with Candida and, after prolonged neutropenia, Aspergillus. Because neutrophils make pus and much of the local inflammatory reaction, signs are muted, and fever may be the only finding; oral ulcers and mucositis are common. Defense against viruses depends mainly on lymphocytes and is relatively preserved.

blocks.title: Mechanisms of neutropenia
rows: Aplastic anemia, leukemia, metastatic infiltration, megaloblastic anemia, radiation
Other cell lines usually low too
Immune destruction or direct toxicity to precursors; abrupt fever and sore throat
Autoimmune neutropenia, systemic lupus erythematosus, Felty syndrome (rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly), neonatal alloimmune neutropenia
Antibodies or T cells remove neutrophils; Felty syndrome adds splenic sequestration
Cells pooled in an enlarged spleen
Cyclic neutropenia (ELANE), severe congenital neutropenia (ELANE, HAX1)
Promyelocyte apoptosis; continuous maturation arrest in the congenital form
blocks.caption: Neutropenia arises from low production, destruction, or redistribution.

blocks.text: Cyclic neutropenia is usually autosomal dominant and caused by mutations in ELANE, the gene for neutrophil elastase. Mutant elastase misfolds and triggers the unfolded protein response and apoptosis in promyelocytes, and, for reasons not fully explained, the count oscillates with a period of about 21 days, with neutropenia lasting several days in each cycle, typically bringing fever, mouth ulcers, and infections. Other ELANE mutations cause the more severe, continuous severe congenital neutropenia. An important exception is the lower ANC seen in many healthy people of African or Middle Eastern ancestry who have the Duffy-null red cell phenotype; neutrophil production and function are normal, and infection risk is not increased.

sections.title: Leukemoid reaction versus chronic myeloid leukemia

blocks.text: A leukemoid reaction is an exaggerated, normal response of the marrow, usually a white count above about 50,000/µL, to severe infection (for example Clostridioides difficile colitis or tuberculosis), sepsis, hemorrhage, acute hemolysis, or a tumor that secretes G-CSF. G-CSF and other cytokines speed release of marrow neutrophils and shorten maturation, so less mature forms enter the blood. This is the left shift: more bands, with metamyelocytes and occasional myelocytes. Cells released early show toxic granulation (prominent primary granules), Döhle bodies (patches of residual rough endoplasmic reticulum), and cytoplasmic vacuoles. Activated, polyclonal neutrophils have a high LAP score, and the count falls once the cause resolves.

Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm defined by BCR-ABL1, the fusion gene formed by the reciprocal translocation t(9;22) that creates the Philadelphia chromosome. The fusion protein is a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives proliferation and resists apoptosis. The clone matures, so the blood shows granulocytes at every stage, with peaks of myelocytes and segmented neutrophils and few blasts in chronic phase. Basophilia and often eosinophilia and thrombocytosis are characteristic, and the spleen is enlarged. The clonal neutrophils have a low LAP score. Without control, CML progresses to an accelerated phase and then a blast crisis resembling acute leukemia.

Increased; basophilia is a key clue
blocks.caption: Basophilia, low LAP, and splenomegaly point to CML; demonstrating BCR-ABL1 confirms it.

blocks.text: LAP is not specific to one disease. It is high in PV and in pregnancy, and low in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, so it supports rather than proves a diagnosis, and molecular testing for BCR-ABL1 has largely replaced it. A leukemoid reaction should also be distinguished from a leukoerythroblastic picture, in which nucleated red cells and immature granulocytes appear because the marrow is infiltrated or fibrotic rather than stimulated.

integration.text: Each disorder in this chapter is a failure of supply, signal, or stem cell. Supply failures come from gut anatomy and biochemistry: iron is absorbed in the duodenum, folate in the jejunum, and B12 in the terminal ileum after binding a gastric protein, so celiac disease, gastrectomy, atrophic gastritis, Crohn disease, and a tapeworm each predict a specific deficiency. Heme and thymidine pathways explain the cell size, with too little hemoglobin making small cells and too little DNA synthesis making large ones. Signal failures involve hepcidin, erythropoietin, and G-CSF, which link inflammation, renal oxygen sensing, and infection to blood counts. Stem cell failures range from immune destruction in aplastic anemia to clonal growth in PV and CML.

Immunology and microbiology recur throughout: autoantibodies against parietal cells and neutrophils, cytotoxic T cells against stem cells, and IL-6 against iron availability, while neutropenia sets up infection with endogenous bacteria and fungi. Ferritin, LAP, MCV, and the first hemoglobin after bleeding can all mislead when inflammation, coexisting deficiencies, or time course are ignored, so values are read together with the smear and the clinical setting.

summary: Iron deficiency lowers ferritin first, then raises TIBC and lowers saturation, and finally produces a microcytic hypochromic anemia with a high RDW.
In anemia of chronic disease, IL-6 induces hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and traps iron in macrophages, so ferritin is normal or high and TIBC is low.
Thalassemia trait has normal iron studies, a high red cell count, and target cells; sideroblastic anemia has high iron and ringed sideroblasts.
Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, raising ALA and zinc protoporphyrin, and inhibits pyrimidine 5' nucleotidase, causing basophilic stippling.
B12 deficiency traps folate and blocks methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so megaloblastic anemia comes with high methylmalonic acid and subacute combined degeneration.
Folate deficiency gives the same megaloblastic blood picture within months, with high homocysteine, normal methylmalonic acid, and no neurologic damage.
Aplastic anemia is stem cell failure, usually T cell mediated, with pancytopenia, low reticulocytes, a fatty marrow, and no splenomegaly.
PV has JAK2 V617F and low erythropoietin; secondary polycythemia has high erythropoietin, appropriate with hypoxia and inappropriate with tumors; relative polycythemia has a normal red cell mass.
After acute hemorrhage the hemoglobin falls only as plasma volume is restored, and reticulocytes peak at about 7 to 10 days; chronic loss causes iron deficiency.
An ANC below 500/µL carries a high risk of bacterial and fungal infection; a leukemoid reaction has high LAP and toxic granulation, while CML has basophilia, low LAP, and BCR-ABL1.

verify: Reference ranges for ferritin, serum iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation, and RDW vary by laboratory; confirm the values NABNE uses.
Ferritin cutoffs for iron deficiency differ between sources (about 15 versus 30 ng/mL, and up to about 100 ng/mL with inflammation).
Polycythemia vera hemoglobin and hematocrit thresholds follow the WHO classification (16.5 g/dL or 49% in men, 16.0 g/dL or 48% in women); confirm the edition NABNE follows.
Timing of reticulocytosis after hemorrhage (onset about 3 to 5 days, peak about 7 to 10 days) is given slightly differently across sources.
Definitions of hypersegmented neutrophils differ (six or more lobes in any cell versus five lobes in more than 5% of neutrophils).
Confirm whether NABNE materials use the current name Dibothriocephalus latus or the former Diphyllobothrium latus.
The Mentzer index cutoff of 13 is a screening heuristic; confirm whether NABNE expects it.
The leukemoid reaction threshold (white count above about 50,000/µL) varies between sources.
A diagram of iron absorption and hepcidin control (enterocyte, ferroportin, macrophage) would help; request a new diagram name if one is added.
